subject: treasureChest
pitch: A pirate's treasure chest with its lid thrown open. Weathered dark wood planks bound with rusty iron straps and studs, a heavy padlock hanging loose, and spilling out of it: gold coins, a pearl necklace, a jewelled goblet and a few red and green gems. A small skull-and-crossbones is carved on the front.
reasoning:
I'm planning the structure as a single TypeScript module: a root joint since part() requires one, then a hinge joint for the lid parented to the root at the back edge, with the chest body itself modeled as a prop.

For dimensions, I'm sizing the chest around 0.9m wide, 0.55m deep, 0.5m tall body, with the lid opening to roughly 110 degrees. I'm sketching out a wood paint approach using a grain texture for the planks with dark weathered tones, possibly layering plank seam lines along the x-axis for extra detail.

For materials, I'm deciding on a rusty mottled iron for fittings, a warm gold tone for accents, and red/green jewel colors with a pearl highlight—keeping the jewelled goblet accent to red and green gems against gold metal.

For the chest body, I'm realizing a solid box won't work for an open chest, so I need to build it as separate hollow walls—floor, front, back, and sides—so the interior is visible rather than filled solid.

Then for the loot inside, I'm planning a pile of gold coins using small flattened cylinders scattered randomly within the interior bounds, keeping the count around 60 to stay well under part and triangle limits.

For the necklace, I'll use a string of tiny pearl-like spheres arranged along a curved arc, positioning them near the mound inside the chest.

For the goblet I'm designing a lathe profile with points tracing bowl, stem, and foot curves, placed upright on the coin pile and painted in gold tones.

Now I'm adding small red gem spheres around the goblet bowl at a set radius and height, then scattering octahedron gems (red and green) on top of the coins and outside the chest on the floor. I'm also starting on a skull shape placed on the chest's front wall using a sphere base.

Adding iron straps next: vertical bands across the front, back, and lid with small stud spheres, plus a hasp and loose-hanging padlock positioned on the lower-right front.

Now I'm setting up the lid as a hinged piece at the back top edge, working out the joint axis and local coordinates so it swings open around 110 degrees from the hinge.

Working through the lid's hinge point at the front edge, I compute that rotating by -110° moves it up by about 0.51 and back by about 0.18, which puts the open lid leaning back past vertical — a plausible open position of roughly 110°.

I'm structuring the lid as its own joint positioned at the hinge, built in closed pose first, then posing it with a rotation around the x-axis, since the joint's default orientation matches model space. Parts attached to the lid via the bone option should move correctly with this pose, while the root-level contents like coins stay stationary inside — I just need to make sure the pose happens after the lid is built so nothing overlaps in its closed state.

Now I'm working out the lid's actual shape: trying a slab box versus a rounded half-cylinder dome for a nicer curved look, figuring out the right center position relative to the hinge and body height, and deciding how to rotate the cylinder geometry so its axis runs along x instead of y to form the curved half-arc.

That's too tall, so I should flatten the dome by scaling it down in height after rotating, aiming for a shallower lid curve.

The lid spans from y=0 to about 0.11 as a half-ellipse, with the hinge positioned at the back edge where z=-0.28 and y=0.42, giving a joint point I can use to position the lid correctly relative to the model's coordinate system.

I'm placing the lid geometry as a part attached to the lid bone/joint, so moving the joint moves the whole lid mesh. Now I need to figure out how to paint plank seams onto the lid's curved surface, likely using the same wood-paint approach oriented along the z-axis.

Adding iron straps across the dome...

Sketching strap geometry...

Now I'm placing the front and back body straps near the front wall's outer face, figuring out x positions so they don't collide with the skull decoration or the padlock hasp—considering offsets like -0.28 and 0.28 while leaving room for a possible middle strap.

Defining box geometry for floor, front/back/side walls, then placing front straps just outside the front wall surface.

Now I'm designing the front skull-and-crossbones plaque: a darker plate mounted on the front wall, with a cream skull built from a sphere, jaw box, and black eye sockets, plus starting to position a crossbone rod beneath it.

Adjusting the crossbones position slightly so they sit just below the skull's jawline without overlapping. I'm assigning colors now — dark carved plaque, bone-white skull, near-black eye sockets — then starting on the padlock's hasp geometry positioned below the lid edge.

Working out the loose hanging lock: placing the hasp on the front wall, then the lock body hanging off it with an open shackle ring modeled as a torus positioned vertically so it reads as hanging freely from the hasp.

For the coins, I'm thinking cylindrical shapes with a mottled gold paint blending two tones for a worn metallic look.

For the pile, I'm scattering about 80 coins inside the chest within the interior bounds, using a mound-shaped height falloff so coins pile up higher toward the center and taper near the edges, with slight random tilts and layering for a natural heap.

Then I'm adding a few coins and gems spilling out onto the floor in front of the chest at lower height, plus draping a pearl necklace in a soft U-curve across the top of the mound using small spaced spheres.

For the goblet, I'm positioning it resting on top of the coin pile and defining its lathe profile — a narrow base widening into a stem, then flaring into a bowl shape at the top with a slightly wider rim, left unsmoothed for faceted metal look.

I'm adding decorative gems: small red and green spheres studded around the goblet's bowl at set angles, plus scattered stylised gem shapes (octahedrons) in red and green randomly placed across the coin pile and on the floor nearby, using a seeded RNG for consistent placement. I'm also noting there's a chest to place on the ground.

For the chest, I'm confirming it sits flush at floor level, then adding iron details: small rivet-like studs along the front straps using a mottled rusty-iron paint pattern, with the straps themselves painted in a darker mottled brown-black tone for a weathered metal look.

Now I'm working out the geometry for the lid strap sweep, building it as a curved path along an elliptical arc (using z and y semi-axes matching the lid's curvature) so the strap follows the lid's dome shape and meets the chest edges correctly—generating the catmull spline points for this arc...

Checking the rotation and scaling order: after rotating the cylinder, scaling y stretches the dome height correctly, and the length along x still matches the lid's 0.9 span to line up with the body. Now I need to verify the dome radius of 0.28 against the body's z extent to make sure they align properly.

For the lid joint, I'm placing the mesh geometry in model space at [0,0.42,0] while the pivot sits at [0,0.42,-0.28], so the pose rotation of -110° around the X axis will swing the lid open around that pivot point — I'm working through the trigonometry to confirm the dome center lands in the right spot after rotation.

Checking the math, the lid center shifts to about y=0.68 with a slightly negative z, meaning the lid tilts back roughly 20° past vertical when fully open, which matches how chest lids typically open to 100-110°.

Now I'm considering whether to add hinge hardware — maybe a small iron rod across the back at z=-0.28, attached to the lid bone so it rotates along with the lid.

Confirming the hinge pin sits along the rotation axis so it stays invariant through the rotation, then moving on to think about front strap placement near the lock and the wood paint setup for the body boxes. I'm setting up the imports needed from three.js and the custom builder utilities, including geometry types and helper functions like grain, mottle, paint, catmull, and rng.

Adding grain pattern and gold/iron coloring...

Settling on plain dark grey metal for the padlock. Now I'm writing a helper function to create box-shaped parts attached to the root bone, so I can build up the wooden body piece by piece.

Defining the root and lid joints explicitly with their positions and parent relationships so the lid parts rig correctly instead of being grabbed by the nearest joint heuristic.

I'm setting the lid's role as a hinge so its rotation axis aligns with its local X, then posing it with a negative rotation to swing it open. For the strap sweeps, I'm binding them to the lid bone directly and generating their paths with catmull curves through a sweep function.

Now I'm adding small stud spheres along the top of each strap arc, plus scattering around 70 gold coins using cylinder geometry with randomized position and tilt rotations, each bound to the root.

Wall top sits around 0.42, so coins piling up to 0.165 stay within bounds. I'm also scattering some coins spilling outside the mound onto the floor near the front edge, placing them at low height with random x/z positions.

I'm giving these floor coins slight random tilt rotations so they lie mostly flat but look naturally scattered rather than perfectly stacked, letting them sink slightly into the floor for realism.

Now I'm positioning the pearl necklace draped over the mound — 18 spheres placed along an x-range with a y-height that follows the mound's curve so it looks like it's resting naturally rather than floating.

I'm placing the goblet near the necklace's start point at a height roughly matching the mound's surface there, settling it in slightly for a grounded look. For the gems, I'm scattering some across the top of the coin pile with a bit of y-variance so they sit believably, and planning another cluster of gems on the floor just in front of the mound.

Now I'm designing the skull-and-crossbones ornament on the front face: a plaque box offset from the strap positions so they don't overlap, a sphere skull with a jawbone box beneath it, small dark spheres for eyes and a tiny nose box, then two crossed bone rods running diagonally behind it to form the classic crossbones shape.

I'm working out bone attachment for these decorative parts—since they're all near the root joint rather than the lid joint based on distance calculations, I'll explicitly assign them to the "root" bone to be safe. Now I'm starting on the padlock body as the next sub-component.

Placing the padlock's body, shackle ring, and hasp pieces, I'm adjusting their positions so the ring overlaps correctly with the hasp to look hooked through it—nudging the ring's vertical center down slightly to make the attachment read naturally.

I'm positioning the front straps and their studs, checking widths and spacing so the straps clear the lock hasp and plaque without overlapping.

Now I'm working out side straps, back straps, and hinge placement relative to wall thickness, then skipping a bottom iron band and confirming wood wall depths. For the lid straps, I'm setting up a sweep along an arched path using sine/cosine points so the strap curves correctly over the lid's rounded profile.

Checking the catmull path import resolves correctly from the builder library, and noting the strap material should use iron paint. For the hinge pin, I'm placing an iron rod spanning the back edge at the lid's pivot point, verifying its axis aligns exactly with the rotation joint so the lid swings properly around it.

Finally I'm sketching out the module structure: a meta export with the chest's name and description, then a default export function that creates the builder, assembles all the parts in order (lid pieces before the pose step), and applies skinning/pose logic last before returning the root.

Now I'm working out the treasure contents—coins and gems using octahedron and cylinder geometries—and the goblet shape via a lathe revolve with gold coloring, placing gem accents around its bowl using angular offsets and alternating red/green octahedron gems bound to the root bone.

I'm double-checking the lid geometry: wood plank seams calculated from the dome's y-levels, strap-iron placement, and pose rotation types for the hinge. I'm verifying the cylinder-based dome construction—using scale and rotation to form a half-ellipse profile matching the body's width, confirming it sits correctly atop the closed chest in the 0.42–0.532 y-range.

Now I'm planning the paint functions (mottle, grain) and tallying part counts across coins, gems, pearls, and body pieces to estimate total scene complexity around 150 parts before writing the final clean code. Setting up a helper function for placing parts...

Still writing placement logic...

Adding studs, side straps, and the front plaque geometry...

Adjusting eye position slightly inward so they sit on the skull's front surface, then placing a small nose box and considering where the crossbones rod sits relative to the plaque front.

I'm checking that the crossbones fit within the plaque's vertical span and stick out enough at the front to read clearly, while staying clear of the jaw below.

Now I'm placing the padlock mechanism itself — body, hanging ring, and hasp — positioning them so the lock sits flush against the straps without clipping, and visually "hangs loose" from the ring as expected.

Then I'm shifting to the lid straps, sweeping a curved tube profile along an arc for each of three x-positions to form the metal bands wrapping over the lid's dome.

Adding stud and hinge pin placement...

The hinge pin sits at the back wall edge, poking out slightly past it with its small radius, which should be fine placement-wise. For the coins, I'm placing small cylinder shapes with gold material scattered at various positions and rotations.

For the overall scene, I'm planning a 70-coin interior mound plus scattered floor coins spilling out the open front of the chest, around 16 pieces at slight random tilts near ground level. Then I'll scatter a handful of red and green gem clusters both within the mound and a few more spilled onto the floor in front, varying their height and position randomly for a natural scattered look.

I'm working out placement for a pearl necklace draped across the hoard using a sine curve for the strand shape, plus a goblet positioned toward the back-left with alternating red and green gems arranged in a hexagonal ring around its bowl. I'll give the goblet a gold lathe material with extra segments for smoothness, then finalize the random seed for reproducibility.

Setting up imports and a helper function to simplify placing parts with position and bone options, defining sphere geometry for small decorative elements, and starting a pose adjustment for the lid's rotation axis.

I'm finishing the lid rotation setup and returning the root bone, confirming the root joint doesn't need a parent reference, and checking that the wood paint works correctly on the lid's cylinder geometry since it already has proper normals. I'm doing a final pass to make sure there aren't any unused variables that would cause issues.
